entities.summary:
Bomilcar (died 307 BCE) emerged as a prominent Carthaginian general during the tumultuous Third Sicilian War, a protracted conflict that decisively shaped the geopolitical landscape of the Central Mediterranean in the late 4th century BCE. His career, spanning the final decades of the Classical era, was intrinsically linked to Carthage's enduring struggle against the Greek city-states of Sicily, particularly Syracuse under the ambitious tyrant Agathocles. Beyond the battlefield, Bomilcar's significance is underscored by his audacious, albeit failed, attempt to seize dictatorial power within Carthage itself, exposing the deep-seated political tensions and oligarchic vulnerabilities of the Punic republic.

His military career saw him leading Carthaginian forces in Sicily, most notably against Agathocles. In 310 BCE, following Agathocles' daring invasion of North Africa, Bomilcar was one of the two generals commanding the Carthaginian defense, engaging the Syracusan forces near White Tunis. Despite initial successes and the numerical superiority of the Carthaginian army, internal discord and a lack of decisive action allowed Agathocles to maintain his foothold. Later, in 307 BCE, while commanding troops within Carthage, Bomilcar orchestrated a coup, attempting to capitalize on the city's wartime anxieties and perceived weaknesses of its ruling aristocratic council. He marched his forces into the city, executing political opponents and aiming to establish a tyranny, a move reminiscent of the Greek tyrants he often fought.
